title: What Happens If a Spacecraft Tries to Land on Ice Giant Uranus?
description:
Why Knocked-Sideways Uranus Has 21-Year Winters

What happens if a spacecraft dives beneath those clouds to land on the ice below? As an ice giant, Uranus has no true surface. Beneath the hydrogen and helium clouds, 80% or more of the planet's mass is a hot, dense fluid of water, methane, and ammonia above a small rocky core — and near that core, Uranus heats up to 9,000 degrees Fahrenheit (4,982 degrees Celsius).

Sources: NASA Science, Uranus Facts — ice giant interior with no true surface, ≥80% hot dense fluid of water, methane, and ammonia above a small rocky core, and 9,000 °F (4,982 °C) core temperature (https://science.nasa.gov/uranus/facts/) · NASA NSSDCA, Uranus Fact Sheet — 82.5% H2, 15.2% He, and 2.3% CH4 upper atmosphere and interior structure (https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/uranusfact.html).

Pictures: NASA/JPL Voyager 2 (PIA18182, PIA01488), NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope NIRCam (weic2332a, weic2310a), and NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope WFC3/OPAL (STScI-H-p1906a, STScI-H-p1906c) alongside original animated explainers, with AI-assisted voice and editing. Facts: every number is checked against the sources listed above.
Image credits: NASA/JPL-Caltech (Voyager 2, PIA18182, PIA01488); NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Joseph DePasquale (STScI) (weic2332a, weic2310a); NASA, ESA, A. Simon (NASA GSFC), M.H. Wong and A. Hsu (UC Berkeley) (STScI-H-p1906a, STScI-H-p1906c).
